title: Anti-MuSK-Positive Myasthenia Gravis in a Patient with Parkinsonism and Cognitive Impairment
case_prompt:
A 73-year-old man was admitted for rapidly progressive bulbar dysfunction with severe dysphagia requiring a gastric tube, dysarthria, nasal speech, and ophthalmoplegia without ptosis. Over the preceding two years he had experienced similar remitting–relapsing episodes, each resolving spontaneously in days to weeks, and in the prior three months he had been hospitalized twice for severe dysphagia. Initial investigations—including acetylcholine‐receptor antibodies, autoimmune and inflammatory screening, barium swallow study, fibroscopy, and neck CT—were normal, and his response to three days of IV methylprednisolone during a relapse was inconsistent.

At age 70 he had developed an asymmetrical, progressive rest tremor in his legs. A brain MRI at that time was normal, and treatment with levodopa–carbidopa produced no significant improvement. On current examination he had a masked face with decreased blinking, an astonished look, external ophthalmoplegia with partial downward gaze sparing without diplopia, weak forced eye closure, severe lower cranial‐nerve involvement with dysphagia, hypophonia, nasal speech, and marked tongue weakness. The pharyngeal reflex was normal; the masseter reflex was brisk. Frontal release signs (glabellar, orbicularis oris, palmomental) were present. There was an asymmetrical, predominantly left‐sided rest tremor in both legs; strength and osteotendinous reflexes were otherwise normal except for areflexia in the left upper limb, and plantar responses were flexor. Axial rigidity was evident, and gait showed en-bloc turning and freezing.

Laboratory studies showed normal biochemistry including creatine kinase; an initial serum lactate of 2.5 mmol/L was not confirmed on repeat (0.9 mmol/L). Antineuronal (Hu-Yo-Ri), anti-AChR, and voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies were negative. Chest CT, spirometry, and pulmonary assessment were unremarkable. Neurophysiological studies—including limb EMG/ENG, low-rate repetitive nerve stimulation, and single-fiber EMG of the facial nerve—were normal. CSF examination, including beta-amyloid and total and phosphorylated tau proteins, was normal. A right biceps muscle biopsy showed atrophy of type I and II fibers without COX or SDH abnormalities. Brain MRI showed mild temporal lobe atrophy and small frontal white-matter lesions. FDG PET revealed decreased metabolism in the brainstem and medial temporal cortex. Neuropsychological testing demonstrated a mild subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction (reduced verbal fluency, impaired planning and execution, and constructive apraxia).

A few days after admission he improved spontaneously, the gastric tube was removed, and he received IV methylprednisolone (1 g/day for three days) followed by oral prednisolone (50 mg/day with taper) with only mild benefit.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. A broad neuromuscular and structural workup ruled out other peripheral and metabolic causes — “A complete diagnostic workup including serum lactate determination, muscle biopsy, CSF examination, and cerebral MRI with DWI sequences excluded other differential diagnosis including Lambert Eaton syndrome, mitochondrial disorders, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP), motor neuron disease and brainstem ischemia.”  
2. Parkinson’s disease was considered but excluded — “Parkinson's disease was excluded for the absence of clinical criteria.”  
3. Vascular parkinsonism and vascular cognitive impairment were excluded by imaging — “The cerebral MRI, showing only aspecific small frontal white matter lesions, was not consistent with a vascular parkinsonism and a vascular cognitive impairment.”  
4. Progressive supranuclear palsy was considered but clinical criteria were not met — “the clinical course in this patient did not satisfy clinical criteria for PSP, which require a gradually progressive course in addition to supranuclear gaze palsy and postural instability with falls.”  
5. MuSK-antibody–positive myasthenia gravis was confirmed by serology — “high titres of anti-MuSK (muscle-specific tyrosine kinase) antibodies were found.”
